issues.legal_issue: A buyer who has paid purchase money under a genuine sale agreement has a charge over the seller’s interest in the property for that money and interest, enforceable against the seller and persons claiming under the seller.
material_facts: Purchasers entered into sale agreements for proposed space and paid purchase money in anticipation of delivery.
The agreements were genuine, and the purchasers had not improperly declined delivery.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers had a statutory charge over the seller’s interest in the property for the purchase money paid and interest on it, enforceable against the seller and persons claiming under the seller.
issues.legal_principle: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 55(6)(b), creates the buyer’s charge in the absence of a contract to the contrary, provided the buyer has not improperly declined delivery. The charge is statutory, distinct from a contractual charge (Chettiar Firm v. Chettiar), and requires a genuine agreement (T.N. Hardas v. Babulal). It is enforceable against persons claiming under the seller; the 1929 amendment removed the former requirement that such persons have notice of the payment.

rule.if: purchaser_claim_under_sale_agreement and genuine_sale_agreement and purchase_money_paid_in_anticipation_of_delivery and not buyer_improperly_declined_delivery

predicates.purchaser_claim_under_sale_agreement: A buyer seeks to enforce rights arising from an agreement to purchase property.
predicates.genuine_sale_agreement: The agreement to sell the property is genuine.
predicates.purchase_money_paid_in_anticipation_of_d: The buyer paid purchase money before delivery of the property.
predicates.buyer_improperly_declined_delivery: The buyer improperly refused to accept delivery of the property.

issues.definition: When a buyer brings a claim under a genuine sale agreement, has paid purchase money in anticipation of delivery, and has not improperly refused delivery, the buyer has a charge over the seller’s interest for the purchase money and interest.

issues.legal_issue: A buyer’s charge over property follows the property or money into which the charged property is converted.
material_facts: The purchasers’ claims concerned property and proposed building space that were not delivered to them.
The property and structure were taken over and later transferred to a purchaser for consideration, converting the original property into money.
issues.conclusion: The charge may be enforced against substituted property or money into which the charged property has been converted.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the general principle that a charge follows the subject matter when it is converted into another form. Section 73 of the Transfer of Property Act is an example of that principle. The principle had been applied to substituted mortgage securities in Barham Deo Prasad v. Tara Chand and Muniappa v. Subbaiah, and applies equally to a statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b).

predicates.purchaser_claim_under_sale_agreement: A buyer seeks to enforce rights arising from an agreement to purchase property.
predicates.buyer_has_charge_over_property: The buyer has a charge over the property for amounts paid in anticipation of delivery.
predicates.charged_property_converted_into_other_pr: The property subject to the charge is converted into other property or money.

issues.definition: If a buyer pursuing a sale-agreement claim has a charge over property and that property is converted into other property or money, the charge follows the substituted property or money.

issues.legal_issue: A buyer who has paid purchase money in anticipation of delivery is entitled to interest on that money until delivery or execution of the sale deed, whichever occurs first.
material_facts: Purchasers paid purchase money for proposed property that was not delivered to them.
The Court had previously directed full reimbursement of purchasers, including interest for purchasers who bought before the restriction on further sales and purchasers who bought afterward.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers were entitled to interest on the purchase money from the date of payment until delivery of the property or execution of the sale deed, whichever occurred earlier.
issues.legal_principle: Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act entitles a buyer to interest on purchase money paid in anticipation of delivery, subject to the statutory conditions. The Court also relied on its earlier judgment directing full reimbursement, including interest, for both earlier and later purchasers.

predicates.purchaser_claim_for_reimbursement: A buyer seeks reimbursement of money paid under a property sale agreement.
predicates.purchase_money_paid_in_anticipation_of_d: The buyer paid purchase money before delivery of the property.
predicates.property_not_delivered_to_buyer: The buyer did not receive delivery of the property.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeks reimbursement after paying purchase money in anticipation of delivery and the property was not delivered, the buyer is entitled to interest on that money.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to enforce a statutory charge over immovable property is governed by the limitation period for enforcing money secured by a charge.
material_facts: The purchasers sought to enforce the statutory charge arising from their payments under sale agreements.
The claim concerned money secured by a charge on immovable property.
issues.conclusion: The period for enforcing the statutory charge is twelve years from when the money becomes due, including when the charge is enforced against substituted security.
issues.legal_principle: Article 62 of the Limitation Act, 1963, provides twelve years to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage or otherwise charged upon immovable property, running from when the money becomes due. The Court held that this applies to a statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act and to enforcement against substituted security, rather than the three-year period.

predicates.claim_to_enforce_statutory_property_char: A claimant seeks to enforce a statutory charge over property.
predicates.money_secured_by_charge_on_immovable_pro: The money claimed is secured by a charge on immovable property.

issues.definition: A claim to enforce a statutory property charge securing money on immovable property is governed by the limitation period for enforcing charged money.

issues.legal_issue: A seller that fraudulently accepts payments from more buyers than available units, without disclosing the contingent nature of the agreements, cannot rely on a contractual term excluding interest.
material_facts: The seller accepted bookings from nearly three times as many buyers as there were available units and collected substantial sums.
The buyers were not adequately informed that their agreements depended on the availability of units.
The agreements contained a term purporting to exclude interest if the transaction failed, and the Court had already found fraud in the seller’s conduct.
issues.conclusion: The seller could not rely on the no-interest term to defeat the purchasers’ claims for interest.
issues.legal_principle: Although Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act operates in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the Court held that a seller found to have acted fraudulently could not rely on such a term to avoid interest. Accepting bookings in excess of available units without adequate notice of their contingent nature was fraudulent and unfair; excluding interest in those circumstances was unconscionable. The Court relied on its earlier finding of fraud and its earlier direction that purchasers be reimbursed in full with interest.

rule.if: purchaser_claim_for_interest and seller_accepted_bookings_exceeding_available_units and buyers_not_told_agreements_were_contingent and contract_excludes_interest and seller_found_to_have_committed_fraud

predicates.purchaser_claim_for_interest: A buyer seeks interest on money paid under a property sale agreement.
predicates.seller_accepted_bookings_exceeding_avail: The seller accepted bookings from more buyers than there were available units.
predicates.buyers_not_told_agreements_were_continge: The buyers were not adequately told that their agreements depended on unit availability.
predicates.contract_excludes_interest: The agreement contains a term purporting to exclude interest if the transaction fails.
predicates.seller_found_to_have_committed_fraud: The seller was found to have committed fraud in connection with the transactions.

issues.definition: If a buyer claims interest under an agreement excluding interest and the seller fraudulently accepted excess bookings without disclosing their contingent nature, the seller cannot rely on the exclusion term.

issues.legal_issue: A general public warning about sales does not, by itself, defeat later purchasers’ entitlement to interest where the Court has already directed their full reimbursement and individual notice is difficult to establish.
material_facts: The later purchasers had paid money for proposed property after a public warning about further sales had been published.
The Court considered it difficult to determine which purchasers had actually seen the warning.
An earlier judgment had directed full reimbursement of later purchasers.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to revisit the earlier determination that later purchasers were entitled to interest; the public warning did not defeat that entitlement.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on its earlier judgment directing full reimbursement of later purchasers and observed that individual purchasers’ knowledge of a public notice was difficult to prove. It therefore declined to reconsider the previously determined entitlement to interest.

predicates.later_purchaser_claim_under_prior_reimbu: A later purchaser seeks reimbursement under an earlier court direction covering later purchasers.
predicates.public_warning_about_sales_published: A public warning was published about further sales of the property.
predicates.individual_purchaser_notice_is_difficult: It is difficult to establish whether an individual purchaser received or saw the public warning.

issues.definition: When a later purchaser claims under an earlier reimbursement ruling, publication of a warning does not defeat interest entitlement if individual notice is difficult to establish.
